t: First, the rule that never changes
x: The rule Q: What keeps a trade route open? A: Not law and not distance. Somebody strong enough to be there, paying the running cost every day, whether or not anything happens. Q: What happens when several powers can close a route and none can afford to hold it open? A: Safety stops being a guarantee and becomes a schedule. You are covered at certain hours and you carry the risk the rest of the time. Think of it like this. A night bus runs through a rough district, and the police used to patrol it all night. Now they patrol from eight to nine and from two to three. Nothing was cancelled and nobody was told. But every driver puts the fare up, and some stop driving. This week the route is the Strait of Hormuz , the narrow sea passage Gulf oil leaves through. The two patrol hours are literal.

t: The whole week as one picture

Sixty-plus were fired in a single night over Jordan to stop twenty, out of perhaps seven or eight hundred left — and they take years to build, which no election shortens. What did the countries nearby do about it? They stopped waiting. Saudi Arabia closed its own pipeline around the Strait — the region's one physical way around it — and did not strike back. It had asked Washington for strikes and got intelligence instead. Why does an oil price change what I pay to borrow? Because fuel raises the price of everything, and lenders charge more when prices rise. American and British long-term rates hit decade highs. Japan is the clearest case: producer prices ran +7.6%, so its central bank raises into an energy shock — the world's last cheap pool of money is being priced up, not down. So what reaches Vietnam? Two things. Fuel, because Vietnam buys crude and refined fuel through that same passage and nobody builds a refinery inside a crisis. And attention: a $114bn surplus with the United States, taxed far below what China pays, is now the most visible line in the American trade accounts. And what would change the answer? The weakest link, and what the picture shows. The mechanism Q: What does a small country win when two giants fight over trade? A: The factories that leave the loser. That prize is real. Q: What does the prize cost? A: The small country becomes the one name that grew on the winner's own list of problems. Think of it like this. Two neighbours quarrel, and the customers of one walk down the road to a small shop. The shop is happy. Then the angry neighbour opens his own books and finds one name that grew. He sends an inspector to ask where the goods on those shelves were made. This week the small shop is Vietnam. It sold the United States $114bn more than it bought, the largest gap of any country. The inspector is a ruling on where a good really comes from. Vietnam sold the United States $114bn more goods than it bought from it in the first half of 2026. That is the largest gap of any country, ahead of Mexico at $103bn and China at $74bn. because Vietnam pays an effective tax of about 6% on those goods, and China pays 23%. So the cheapest factory move on earth still ends in Vietnam. Lowy Institute, Sep 11 So the prize became the danger. The biggest number at the lowest tax rate goes first in line for a ruling on where its goods really come from. because a tax rate is a cost Hanoi can argue down. A ruling on origin says the goods were never Vietnamese, and no tax rate offsets that. Lowy Institute, Sep 11 And that ruling will hit a boom that only outsiders feel. First-half growth of 8.2% came almost entirely from foreign-owned and state-favoured firms, while small Vietnamese firms lost credit and land. because a boom carried by outsiders leaves when the rule on origin changes. East Asia Forum, Sep 11 And shared or not, the boom runs on imported fuel. Brent crude, the world oil price, crossed $100 and then reached $105 as the passage out of the Gulf effectively closed. because Vietnam buys both crude oil and refined fuel through that passage, and nobody can build a refinery inside a crisis. BBC, Sep 10 So Hanoi adds suppliers that nobody can take away. Vietnam's top leader, Tô Lâm, went to Moscow to widen nuclear and oil-and-gas work with Putin, then flew straight on to France. because two capitals on one trip is the whole doctrine. Vietnam does not choose a side. It refuses to have only one. Nikkei Asia, Sep 10 So why go to Moscow, and why now? The report names energy as the purpose and gives no stated reason from Hanoi. The timing is on this page: oil is at $105, the passage is closed, and nobody can build a refinery inside a crisis. because a new supplier is the one insurance that a fuel buyer can still arrange while the passage is closed. Nikkei Asia, Sep 10 What most people miss The loud Vietnam story is the record surplus, and it reads as a win. The quiet one is that the rate producing it is set by how close Washington thinks Hanoi stands, not by what Vietnam sells — and an origin ruling never changes the published rate, so it will move without a headline. Two more items belong in the file. Vietnam's $4bn Cà Mau–Hòn Khoai bridge and dual-use port corridor pushes its contest with China off the water and into Cambodian ground. East Asia Forum, Sep 8 And Chinese soft power among young Vietnamese is compounding fast, with Chinese-language job postings up 50% and students in China roughly doubled since 2018. Fulcrum, Sep 7

The mechanism Q: Why does a neutral country still need its own weapons? A: Because neutrality is not a label that a country announces. It is a defence that the country pays for, and the payment must arrive. Q: What breaks that faster, a war or a bad invoice? A: A bad invoice. A country can argue about a war for years. A price that was never fixed destroys the trust that the paying depends on. Think of it like this. A village votes a tax to build its own fire station. Then the village learns that the builder's fixed price was never fixed, and that one man in the office knew. The fire risk did not change that day. The willingness to pay did, and the station is not built. This week the builder is the American F-35 fighter jet that Switzerland agreed to buy. The tax is a rise in Swiss value-added tax, the sales tax added to most things people buy. Switzerland told its voters the American F-35 jets it agreed to buy came at a fixed price. They did not, and the defence ministry kept saying they did. because a fixed price means the seller swallows any overrun; without one the buyer pays whatever the jets cost. The NZZ found the ministry repeated "fixed" against nearly all the evidence, and one purchasing official knew the real terms. NZZ, Sep 12 So the money followed the trust out. Switzerland was raising its sales tax to fill a special army fund. Senators on the upper house's security committee moved to cut the fund loose from that tax rise. because cutting them apart leaves the army build-up with no source of money — and nobody ever voted to shrink the build-up. It lost its funding as a side effect. NZZ, Sep 10 So why cut it loose, and why now? The committee gave no stated reason. The timing is reported: the fixed-price claim collapsed in the same week. because once the buyer's own numbers are in doubt, no chamber will ask voters for a tax rise to pay that buyer's bills. NZZ, Sep 12 And neutrality lost its main selling point in the same week. The usual argument for staying neutral is that it lets Switzerland trade with everybody. A new analysis found that is not true. because that argument is the commercial case at the centre of the neutrality vote now being campaigned on. Without it, staying neutral is a cost rather than a discount. NZZ, Sep 12 So the voters can see the gap. Only about a third of Swiss voters believe that their politics can react quickly to a global crisis. because they have just watched a fighter price, an army fund and a neutrality argument come apart in one week, with no decision taken on any of them. NZZ, Sep 10 So the central bank is the only Swiss institution left that acts. The chairman of the Swiss National Bank told business leaders that fuel prices are the main reason Swiss inflation rose, and closed on the slide «Märkte erwarten globalen Anstieg der Zinsen» (markets expect a global rise in interest rates). because the bank can act this week without asking anyone. SNB, Sep 11 What most people miss Switzerland argues about neutrality as an identity, and then has the price of it set by a foreign invoice and a foreign interest rate. Nobody voted for either. The deeper miss is the order things happened in: the F-35 affair is not a scandal that delays rearmament — it is the reason the tax that pays for rearmament was just cut loose. The failure moved from the aircraft to the money in four days. That is the second week running that a paid-for European weapons order has quietly turned into no weapons and no money.

The mechanism Q: What does a security promise cost? A: The daily cost of being there, whether or not anything happens that day. Q: What happens when the daily cost is higher than what you can build? A: The promise gets rationed. Nobody cancels it and nobody withdraws it. It arrives in smaller amounts, by the hour. Think of it like this. A landlord promises that the building always has a night watchman. Then the landlord cuts the watchman to two patrols a night. Nobody announced a withdrawal, and the promise is still on paper. But every tenant fits their own lock, and after that the promise is over anyway. This week the landlord is the United States. The two patrols are literal: protection from air attack for tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, cut to two windows a day. Washington cut its protection from air attack for commercial tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow passage that Gulf oil leaves through, to two set windows a day. because the FT reports that the cut came after an increase in Iranian attacks. Cover that used to run all day now comes by the hour, and nobody called it a withdrawal. FT, Sep 12 So why ration the cover, and why now? No stated reason is reported. The missile count is the likely reason: O'Brien counts sixty-plus defensive missiles fired over Jordan on 8 September to stop twenty incoming — out of perhaps seven or eight hundred left in total. because Iran strikes American partner states so that Washington spends its stock defending them. The attacker pays a fraction of each defending shot. Phillips P. O'Brien, Sep 9 So the partners stopped waiting to be defended. Saudi Arabia shut its own East-West pipeline , the line that carried oil around the Strait, after drones launched from Iraq hit it, and did not strike back. because the one physical way around a closed passage was closed by its owner. Holding it open cost more than losing it. BBC, Sep 12 And Washington declined to step in itself. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman pressed Trump directly for American strikes and was offered intelligence and targeting support only. because a day later the Houthis of Yemen took Perim Island at the mouth of the Bab al-Mandab, the passage into the Red Sea, after taking the port of Mokha. A second sea route changed hands because nobody stepped in. BBC, Sep 11 So the war comes home as a household price. American consumer prices rose 3.4% in the year to August as fuel costs squeezed budgets, and Trump said the war and high oil prices will last until after the November elections. because he treats the daily cost as a fixed term that he cannot shorten, and that is an admission. BBC, Sep 11 So borrowing costs rise where the spending cannot stop. The rate the US government pays to borrow for ten years keeps climbing toward 5% despite the finance minister's efforts, and American and British long-term borrowing costs are at their highest in decades. because an oil shock is landing on a government whose debts leave no room, and its lenders are the one opponent that nobody can talk down. NZZ, Sep 11 What most people miss The week reads as escalation — strikes on five Iranian tankers, hard talk at the 9/11 commemoration. Both are cheap. The expensive things all moved the other way: the cover schedule, the unanswered Saudi request, the interceptor count. The tell nobody priced is domestic. A postal service is building a portal to check mail-in ballot envelopes at the November elections NZZ, Sep 7 , and the president has begun promising every adult $5,000 conditional on his party winning BBC, Sep 11 . A country rationing protection abroad is bidding for loyalty at home.

The mechanism Q: How do you gain from a fight you never join? A: You let the other side burn its stock. Then you buy the things it can no longer protect. Q: Is that the same as being strong? A: No. It is being the one whose costs are not rising. That is a different thing, and it ends the moment the other side stops spending. Think of it like this. Two shops on one street run a price war, and both stop repairing their roofs. A third shop across the road sells nothing cheaper and nothing better. It fixes its roof and waits for the rain. This week the third shop is China. The roof is the oil it buys while others fight, and the memory chips it now makes at a profit. China went back into the oil market and bought crude as the fighting in the Strait pushed prices up, though its volumes stay below the level before the war. because it spent the early war using up its stored oil. Nikkei Asia, Sep 11 So why buy now, into a price spike? Nikkei gives no stated reason from Beijing. It reports the timing: the stored oil is run down and the fighting has not stopped. because a buyer who expects a spike to end waits it out. Buying into it is what a country does when it expects the spike to last. Nikkei Asia, Sep 11 So China also gains the industries that the West struggles to hold. The Chinese memory-chip maker CXMT now keeps a larger share of each sale as profit than SK Hynix of Korea or Micron of America. because taking the profit lead in a business that Korea, America and Japan owned for forty years is no longer a story about government money. Nikkei Asia, Sep 10 So Washington's answer to those gains bought the wrong thing. Zeihan reads the roughly $2bn stockpile of minerals that America built as insurance against China: rare earths and gallium come out as side products of other mining, and "70% on average of critical materials processing is done in China". because that makes the stockpile a pile of material that China itself processes, bought as insurance against China. Peter Zeihan, Sep 10 And the one real fix got harder in the same days. Washington banned imports of Canadian spirits, some dairy goods and motorbikes from 29 September, with no trade talks scheduled since negotiations collapsed in late August. because Zeihan names repaired relations with Canada, Australia and Brazil as the real fix: "maybe stop calling it the 51st state". The mineral plan and the trade policy point opposite ways. BBC, Sep 9 But Beijing's grip on its own gains is looser than the headlines say. Its limits on selling rare earths abroad run through provincial governments, regulators and firms that it does not fully command. because that is why this week counts as a small gain for China and not a large one. The gains are real. The control over them is not fully Beijing's. East Asia Forum, Sep 10 What most people miss China's week looks like a run of free wins, and most of them were paid for by somebody else's spending rather than earned. The item to keep is the one that is not free: domestic capital bid a Chinese AI-chip designer up 179% on its first day in Shanghai. Nikkei Asia, Sep 11 That is the same market standing on a single leg that Hồ Quốc Tuấn describes in the West, built inside a closed savings pool — so when the AI group disappoints, China does not escape it either.

Tokyo — it wants to avoid importing a rise in prices it cannot control, and it is stuck because just over 70% of its crude comes through the Strait of Hormuz. Producer prices ran hot in August and import prices in yen jumped, so board member MASU warned the closure can force "a rapid policy interest rate hike", and the Bank of Japan is expected to move to 1.25% on 17–18 September. Money growth stayed modest, which tells you this is a cost shock and not a money shock. What Tokyo cannot do is defend the currency and the export economy at once: the post-intervention rise in the yen has already run past the rate most large manufacturers budgeted for. Berlin — it wants to keep the arrangement Germany has lived under since 1945, and it has just lost the thing that held it. That arrangement had an unwritten rule: Germany does not claim national interests of its own, the way other countries do. Friedman's reading is that the rule lasted only as long as the generation that imposed it, and that generation is gone. The hard-right AfD winning the state of Saxony-Anhalt is the proof. The party is changing shape fast — one of its members of parliament went to Kyiv and says its pro-Moscow wing is going quiet. The same thing is spreading: in Italy a former general is polling sharply upward and pulling the right along with him. Berlin cannot lead Europe's rearmament and lose its own eastern states in the same run of elections. Riyadh — it wants its oil system kept whole, and this week found that the American protection behind it is now advice rather than action. Houthi strikes hit Saudi energy sites, the crown prince asked Washington directly for strikes and received intelligence and targeting help, and then Riyadh shut its own pipeline around the Strait and declined to retaliate. That last decision is the one to read: a country that still believed in American protection would have hit back and let Washington cover it. What Riyadh cannot do is defend a pipeline 1,200km long against drones launched from a neighbouring country, so it took the line out of service instead — and the new Mecca pact — which nobody yet knows will be honoured — is what it has left. Ottawa — it wants customers who are not one angry neighbour, and the numbers are against it. Carney convened a summit to raise $1tn of foreign capital by pitching Canada as the safe place away from its own largest trading partner, in the same week Washington banned Canadian spirits, some dairy and motorbikes from 29 September and nine days after Canada was named an essential minerals partner. A Japanese brewer is already moving production out of Canada into the United States. What Ottawa cannot do is out-wait a policy that gets a domestic political return from the damage.

The part most people miss The place a problem appears is almost never where it was caused, and this week the gap is widest in the dullest document. The Bank of Japan's August producer-price release is not a Japanese story. Import prices in yen up 24.8% is the Strait of Hormuz arriving inside the cost base of the world's largest lender nation, and the interest-rate rise that follows is the last cheap pool of money on earth being made dearer. Every borrower in the world, Vietnam included, pays for that closure through Tokyo without ever reading a Japanese headline. The second miss is an asymmetry that runs under every item above. Closing something is cheap and opening it is ruinous. Drones cost a rounding error against the pipeline they shut. Attacking missiles cost a fraction of the ones fired to stop them. Infantry took a coastline. Against all of that sits weapons production that cannot be sped up inside an election cycle, and a government whose borrowing is getting dearer. This is not a contest of resolve. It is a contest of what things cost to do, and the side making the promises is on the expensive side of it.

Somebody charges, and somebody pays, a published fee to pass through Hormuz or the Bab al-Mandab A closure is a shock that ends. A fee is permanent, and it reaches Vietnam as a standing freight cost that never looks like a security event. If it holds every other country keeps doing what Saudi Arabia, Canada, Japan, Switzerland and Vietnam each did this week: shut its own valves, buy its own suppliers, price its own risk. Nobody announces anything. Costs simply move onto whoever is nearest. If it reverses only two things count, and statements are not among them. Either America funds interceptor production with money set aside for it, or somebody pushes the Houthis off the Bab al-Mandab coast and the Red Sea route reopens at ordinary insurance prices.

The move to copy this week. When something gets more expensive, do not ask who is to blame. Ask who used to pay for it, and what they stopped paying for. Every step on this page came out of that one question. Three questions to ask of any story next week: 1. Who was paying to keep this working — and are they still? 2. If they stopped, who pays instead? It is never nobody. It is whoever is closest and cannot walk away. 3. What would I actually see if I am right? A number, a date or a shipment. Never a statement. Now try it on one we have not answered. Vietnam sells more to the United States than any country on earth and is taxed less for it than China is. Nobody has announced that this will change. Run the three questions on it: who has been paying for that gap, what would make them stop, and what is the first thing you would see — before any headline says so? Write your answer down somewhere. Next week's report will tell you whether it happened, and that is the only way to find out whether your reasoning was right or merely comfortable.

The mechanism Q: Vietnam takes no side. Why does it still get two bills? A: Because the two sides charge for different things. One side sells the fuel that Vietnam burns. The other side buys the goods that Vietnam makes. Q: Can Vietnam pay one bill and refuse the other? A: No. The bills come from different directions, and paying one does not cancel the other. Think of it like this. A small shop sits on a street between two big landlords and pays rent to neither. It still buys its electricity from the first landlord and sells its goods to the tenants of the second. When the first raises the price of electricity and the second starts to check every receipt, the shop pays twice. It never chose a landlord. This week the first landlord is the Gulf, which sold Vietnam 49% of its imported gas before the war. The second landlord is the United States, which is starting to check where Vietnamese goods really come from. Hanoi formally demanded an "immediate cessation" of Chinese building in the Paracel Islands, a group of islands that both countries claim. Because Hanoi owns the legal claim to the islands but not the means to stop the building, and the images show the work is already done. because a formal protest is the move open to a country that owns the claim and not the means to enforce it. The finished airstrip set the date. The Diplomat, Aug 31 So Hanoi buys the means the slow way, by adding partners that no single power can take away. Canada and Vietnam are close to upgrading their partnership. because each new partner among the medium-sized countries lowers Vietnam's dependence on any one great power. This costs little, because it needs nobody's permission. The Diplomat, Sep 1 But partnerships do not pay the fuel bill. Before the Gulf crisis, 49% of Vietnam's gas imports came from the Middle East. because the region's proposed answer is to join its power grids together. Its peso closed at a record low of 62.265 to the dollar, its central bank raised interest rates to 5%, and 2026 inflation is forecast at 6.1% against 1.7% last year. because Manila buys 95% of its oil from the same region. Vietnam sits on the same supply route with a smaller share. The Diplomat, Aug 31 So the bigger danger is the second bill, for selling. America's goods trade gap with 13 Asia-Pacific economies widened to $99.3bn in July, led by Vietnam. because the tax campaign was built to close that gap and failed. The country that leads the gap goes first in line for a customs decision on where its goods really come from. Trigger C10 fires on that. The mechanism Q: Can a country buy safety in advance? A: Only if the order arrives. A signed order is not a weapon. Q: Who sets the delivery date? A: A foreign factory and the customers in the queue ahead of you. Not your budget, and not your vote. Think of it like this. During a dry summer you order a fire door. The joiner takes your money and says the door will come in eight years. You are not poorer, and you are not safer. Nothing you do with your chequebook changes the date. So you make friends with the neighbours who already have doors. This week the joiner is the American factory that builds the Patriot air-defence system. The neighbours are the EU, and the friendship is a seat at their sanctions table. The deal with Berlin to speed up Swiss deliveries of Patriot, the American air-defence missile system, collapsed. Article 4 NATO's "let's talk about this" button. Any member that feels threatened can call all the others into emergency consultation. It is deliberately low-cost — it commits nobody to fight, it just forces a formal conversation. That is why not using it is meaningful: if a country will not even ask for a meeting after being hit, it is telling you something about how much it expects the alliance to do. Transshipment Routing goods through a third country to disguise where they were really made — for example, Chinese goods shipped to Vietnam, relabelled, then exported to the US to dodge tariffs aimed at China. It matters because a transshipment finding is far worse than a tariff: a tariff is a price, but a transshipment ruling can invalidate a country's whole role as a manufacturing alternative. Rate gap The difference between what two countries pay you for holding their money. If the US pays much more than Japan, money flows out of yen into dollars, and the yen falls. Most currency moves are just this gap widening or narrowing — you rarely need any other explanation. The Fed put The market's assumption that if prices fall far enough, the US central bank will step in and cut rates to stop the fall. It is not a written promise — it is a habit investors have come to rely on. When people start doubting it, they take less risk, and prices fall further. Petroline The Saudi pipeline that carries oil across the country to the Red Sea, so tankers can avoid the Strait of Hormuz entirely. It is the main backup route if the Gulf is blocked — which is exactly why threatening it removes the world's spare option. Arbitral Award The 2016 international tribunal ruling that rejected China's expansive South China Sea claims. China refuses to recognise it. Whether a country publicly backs the Award is a low-cost, highly visible test of how far it will go to displease Beijing. China+1 The strategy of keeping factories in China but adding a second country — often Vietnam — to reduce tariff and political risk. Vietnam's export boom largely rides on it, which is why anything that questions Vietnam's independence from China (see **Transshipment**) threatens more than a single tariff line. Neutrality initiative A Swiss popular vote proposal to write strict neutrality into the constitution — which would bind future governments rather than leaving neutrality a matter of policy. Launched from the political right, so left-wing groups backing it is a genuine change in its odds. PMI A monthly survey of purchasing managers, used as an early read on whether an economy is expanding or contracting. Above 50 means growth, below 50 means contraction. Its value is speed — it arrives long before official GDP figures. Section 301 A US trade law letting Washington impose tariffs unilaterally after finding another country's practices unfair. Its significance is procedural: it gives the executive a tariff route that does not need new legislation.
